doc.title: Stab wound: tamponade, PEA and pericardiocentesis
doc.story: A 30-year-old man with a stab wound to the left chest. He arrives tachycardic, with a narrow pulse pressure and a raised CVP; blood is collecting in the pericardium. Without drainage he loses his pulse (PEA) about 8 minutes after arrival. CPR alone cannot bring him back; pericardiocentesis during good CPR brings the pulse back about a minute and a half later.

objectives.text: Name the tamponade within 180 s of arrival from the monitor: tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, CVP above 15 mmHg (instructor-assessed)
Start CPR within 10 s of the pulse loss
Pericardiocentesis within 120 s of starting CPR
Stop CPR (“Pulse back”) within 30 s of the pulse returning on the arterial line and the capnogram
Better: pericardiocentesis before the pulse loss, while the systolic pressure is above 60 mmHg — then no PEA follows

doc.notes: Showcase case (Stage 11). MODELED: the physiology produces every change; the buttons only give what their label says. Measured course and bands: docs/plans/stage-11-scenarios.md.
